text: It all matters. life is about balance, and things don’t always go according to plan. If you can invest early, you give yourself more flexibility later. Just don’t sacrifice your entire present for a future that isn’t guaranteed.

I started saving aggressively in my 20s and 30s. When my dad got sick, I was able to take time away from work to be there for him. That financial flexibility meant more to me than any vacation ever could. Early investing isn’t just about building wealth it’s about buying freedom.

This is so true. Investing early gave me the flexibility to make career choices based on what I actually wanted rather than just what paid the most. The money wasn’t only for retirement; it gave me options along the way.
I’m in my 30s now, and honestly, I wish someone had explained this to me when I was in my 20s.
Better late than never. Take your time, do your research, understand what you’re getting into, and start when you’re ready. Good luck

It’s also about preparing for the unexpected health problems, family responsibilities, career changes, and everything else life can throw at you. Saving and investing early can give you more options when circumstances change.

If you purchased shares of a fund within a Roth, income is not taxed at all.
If you purchased shares of a fund within a rollover (traditional) IRA, all income taken out is considered ordinary income whether the fund calls it ROC, qualified, or ordinary.

You want your base to be in actual qualified dividends and dividend CAGR.  Think SCHD & VIG.  Depending on your portfolio size, you want as small of high yield/capped upside assets as possible.  For example, someone retiring on 800k is going to need a much larger allocation to those high yielding assets than someone with 8 million.  If you need 60k to retire on for example and have 1 million... if you put 50% into VIG & SCHD (average about 2.4%) that would be 12,000.  That would mean you would need 48,000 of income from the remaining 500,000, aka 9.6%.  QQQI is 14%, GPIQ & QDVO are around 10%, GPIX around 8%, IDVO around 5.5%, BTCI around 20% etc.  You could use this "ladder' to mix & match that portfolio.  However if you had 3,000,000 wanting to retire and needed 60k... that's only 2%.  VOO pays 1%.  You could easily hit your goal without any covered calls.  If you're wanting to retire on 2-300,000k, well... you're in a position where you dont need help ha.

Neos has two avenues for generating Return of Capital (ROC). Tax loss harvesting when rolling options, at or prior to expiration, can recharacterize income distributions from unfavorable sources such as ordinary income or short term gains to ROC. The 1256 60/40 Long/Short tax treatment isn't really used to pass along long term gains. Rather, this is another method that Neos uses to carry losses over in the ETF that can again be used to recharacterize income distributions as ROC.

Neos' Garrett has stated in an interview with another YouTuber that they can structure their Flex Options on cash-settled ETF options to make them 1256-eligible, as seems to be the case with the GLD options in IAUI.

For taxable accounts, qualified dividends and long term capital gains are taxed at more favorable rates, but are still included in Adjusted Gross Income (AGI), and thus also in Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI). However, ROC is NOT included in AGI, as well as MAGI. MAGI is used in calculations for things like: 1) Eligibility for various tax credits and deductions; 2) Effects on Roth or Traditional IRA contributions; 3) Qualifications for Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies or Medicaid eligibility; and 4) Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA) Medicare Surcharge tiers for the two-year lookback of investors aged 63 and older.

You missed one of the major fundamental flaws in a covered call fund. When the underlying declines, they continue to follow their playbook to provide a continual steady stream of income to you. What that means, when SPY, QQQ, TSLA, whatever your fund is working off (or a basket of underlyings in the case of something like ULTY) declines in value, they still continue to sell ATM, OTM or whatever their strategy is and as that underlying recovers, you end up getting capped along the way. You will always eventually end up with less NAV then you started with through a complete market cycle. This is why NEOS (who provides the funds mentioned) and many others offers products like their Hedged Equity Income funds or specific strategies to hedge this condition but they return in the single digits. You could protect yourself by running a DIY opportunity hedge upfront and deploying that capital at market lows or putting on second layers of alpha as the market is recovering. You could also run a DIY strategy and control the upside rolls if tested to get back to basis and still make income.
